title: Bullitt's Lick: Kentucky's first industry
summary: Bullitt’s Lick near present-day Shepherdsville was the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the Revolution, starting in 1779.
bodyMarkdown:
Salt was frontier "white gold." Settlers needed it to cure meat and hides, keep livestock healthy, and get through the winter. In the Revolution, Kentucky's biggest supply came from Bullitt's Lick, about three miles west of present-day Shepherdsville in Bullitt County.

The lick took its name from Capt. [Thomas Bullitt](/people/#thomas-bullitt), a Virginia surveyor. In 1773 he came down the Ohio surveying land, and he marked the lick for Col. [William Christian](/people/#william-christian). Buffalo and deer had worn deep trails to the salty ground long before.

Salt making began in 1779. Workers dug wells, drew up the brine, and boiled it in long rows of iron kettles over furnaces. It took hundreds of gallons of brine to make a bushel of salt, and the fires burned day and night. Col. [William Fleming](/people/#william-fleming) visited and wrote that one trough held nearly 2,000 gallons and was emptied three times a day. The [ExploreKYHistory entry](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/888) calls it the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the war.

The work was hard and the woods were dangerous. Cutting wood for the furnaces pulled men away from shelter, and raids came. A fort went up near the lick in 1780 for protection. A rough little town grew around the furnaces. People called it Saltburg.

Pack trains carried salt over the trails to Harrodsburg, the Falls of the Ohio, and other stations. Flatboats took it down the Salt River and on to the Ohio. Salt from Bullitt's Lick went as far as the Illinois country. Its trade helped bring settlers to the neighborhood, and [Shepherdsville](/stories/shepherdsville-on-salt-river/) grew up close by.

Other licks were worked too, like [Mann's Lick](/stories/manns-lick-louisvilles-salt-town/) near Louisville and the [salt works at Drennon Springs](/stories/drennon-springs-salt-works/). In time, deeper wells and cheaper salt from the Kanawha valley and elsewhere undercut the Kentucky works. Bullitt's Lick was mostly shut down by about 1830.

## Kentucky today

A state historical marker in Bullitt County tells the story of the saltworks. The [McAfee Station story](/stories/mcafee-station-on-the-salt-river/) follows the same Salt River country.
